dimensions.name: Reconstructing the Stripe contract & environment

evidence.note: Oriented to the runtime environment (app dir, requirements, offline network check) but this is environment-setup, not Stripe-contract reconstruction.

Task descriptions accurately enumerate the hard contract corners — {type,code,decline_code} error envelope, Stripe test PAN set, idempotency triple (api_key,key,body) incl. cached error replay, webhook re-signing per attempt, PI unexpected_state, restricted-key scopes — showing genuine recall of real Stripe semantics, including the under-specified corners.
Installed the real `stripe` SDK and ran round-trips with api_base pointed at the service, grounding contract fidelity in actual SDK behavior rather than pure guessing.
Edited params.py after SDK smoke tests exposed divergences — findings from real round-trips fed back into the implementation.
Debugged decline replay against the SDK, exercising the cached-error-body idempotency corner it had flagged in planning.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent reconstructs the contract's hard parts accurately from memory — error envelope fields, PAN set, idempotency triple with cached error replay, webhook re-signing, PI state transitions, restricted-key scopes are all named in planning (steps 20-26) — and grounds them by installing the real `stripe` SDK and running round-trips (steps 101+), correcting param handling when divergences surface (109-112). This clears anchor 5's core-contract bar and reaches into anchor 8's coverage of the hard corners grounded in SDK behavior, but it never probes external sources/docs and the cross-checking is memory-first-then-validate rather than the sustained, source-anchored self-correction of anchors 8-10, placing it at a 7.

dimensions.name: Sequencing a large surface + three deep traps

evidence.note: Seven explicit TaskCreate milestones forming an ordered hierarchy: foundation (errors/IDs/store-locks/auth) first, then idempotency, then resource CRUD groups, then PI state machine, billing, webhooks, and finally assembly+smoke. Each carries detailed embedded done-conditions.

The three named traps are each broken out as distinct first-class milestones with concrete acceptance criteria — idempotency (replay incl. error bodies, body-mismatch 400, concurrent serialization, TTL), PI state machine (confirm/capture/cancel + declines), webhook (retry/backoff on 5xx, stop on 4xx, re-sign each attempt) — rather than buried in CRUD.
Explicit dependency ordering: charges/refunds grouped in the PI milestone (23) scheduled before subscriptions/invoices (24), matching the 'charges before refunds before subscription invoices' chain.

Milestones tracked via TaskUpdate in_progress/completed across the full arc, and each trap's done-conditions were later verified by targeted suites (smoke2 idempotency 106-153, webhook_test 175-177, smoke3 billing/refund 179-180) — the plan's acceptance conditions map onto later verification.

Health route / start.sh boot placed in the LAST milestone; first actual boot only at step 99 after all modules were written — the bootable auth'd skeleton was not made verifiable early, the one gap versus ideal de-risking.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent front-loaded and ring-fenced all three high-risk subsystems as first-class milestones each with explicit checks, made cross-resource dependencies explicit (charges/refunds before subscriptions/invoices), scheduled the trickiest semantics (idempotency) early, and carried per-milestone acceptance conditions that later verification suites map directly onto — hitting most of the level-10 description. It falls just short of 10 because the bootable auth'd skeleton was assembled and verified last rather than made runnable early, the one anchor-8 criterion it did not honor.

dimensions.name: SDK-driven, offline compatibility checks

evidence.note: Installs the real stripe SDK and runs smoke.py through stripe.api_base — verifies wire compatibility the way the verifier will, not just curl/200 checks.

Builds smoke2.py for idempotency/subscription/restricted-key, then runs an extended targeted campaign reproducing decline-replay and cached-error-body behavior — active checking of the hardest idempotency semantic.
Dedicated webhook_test.py exercises 5xx retry/backoff; smoke3.py covers pagination, cancel, refund, billing renewal — targeted trap and edge coverage beyond happy paths.
Confirms card decline (invalid PAN → 402 decline), verifying error-mapping semantics.
Re-runs the full smoke 1-3 + webhook suites against fresh/cold-booted start.sh instances — regression discipline so changes don't silently break compatibility.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent verifies through the actual stripe SDK and constructs specific checks for the named traps — idempotency replay including the cached error body (extensively), invalid-PAN decline, webhook 5xx retry/backoff, plus pagination and restricted-key 403 — fully matching the [8] anchor, and adds genuine re-run-after-change regression discipline that gestures toward [10]. It falls short of [10] because the defining concurrency/temporal traps (serialized same-key retries never double-charging, re-signed late webhook acceptance) and the capture-succeeded / same-key-different-body state checks are planned but not evidenced as executed verifications. This lands solidly at 8.

dimensions.name: Tracking coverage across a wide surface

evidence.note: Decomposed the full surface into 7 explicit tasks covering all 12+ resource families plus the three trap subsystems — an accurate up-front done-vs-remaining map of the whole horizon.
Maintained a running checklist via TaskUpdate in_progress→completed for each subsystem across the entire build, sustaining the coverage picture rather than abandoning it midway.

Verification deliberately spanned separate subsystems (smoke1 core, smoke2 idempotency/subs/restricted keys, smoke3 pagination/cancel/refund/billing, webhook_test) — confirming no major area was left unexercised.

Extended circular debugging on stale server processes/port conflicts/billing-interval env — repeatedly killing servers, re-finding PIDs, re-checking default period; the thrashing was not caught or time-boxed early, only resolved late via a _boot.sh helper (step 252).

dimensions.reasoning: The agent kept a genuine, sustained checklist of every endpoint/subsystem and its status (steps 20-26, 29-298) and verified across all resource families, comfortably exceeding anchor 5. But it fell into a prolonged circular debugging loop over server processes and billing config (steps 156-296) that it did not detect or time-box early, which is precisely the stuck/circular pattern anchor 8 requires an agent to catch. That combination — excellent coverage accounting but weak early detection of thrashing — lands it at a 6.

dimensions.name: Course-correcting on compatibility failures

evidence.note: After running the real stripe SDK smoke test, the agent edits params.py twice — indicating SDK form-encoding diverged from its parsing assumption, and it fixed the shared param parser (a correction propagating across all endpoints), rather than pressing on with the wrong model.

Sustained evidence-driven debugging of decline-replay/idempotency: reproduces in isolation, checks logs, and correctly diagnoses that reused idempotency keys and stale servers were confounding the result ('Make idempotency keys unique per run') — distinguishing environment artifact from code bug and preserving verified work.

Billing-renewal test diverged from expectation; agent traces it to duplicate stale server processes binding :8000 with wrong billing-interval env, kills them, and re-confirms default 60s period — root-cause diagnosis, not symptom patching.
When a charge-filter test misbehaved, the agent again investigated running processes/ports and did a clean restart before re-testing, rather than accepting an ambiguous failure.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent never barrels ahead on falsified assumptions: on SDK-driven and trap-related failures it isolates, reproduces, and fixes root causes (params parsing after SDK round-trips; idempotency-key/stale-server confounds; billing env), which clears anchor 5 and the shared param-parser fix shows some cross-endpoint propagation toward anchor 8. However, much of the iteration targets environmental confounds rather than repeated contract-model revisions, and there is no visible evidence of discovering a wrong contract rule (signature scheme, state transition) and structurally re-modeling it — so it falls short of the 8/10 anchors, landing at 6. Confidence is medium because the trajectory exposes only step titles, not the underlying reasoning or observations.

rubric.task_read: A long-horizon, high-complexity build: a single-container service that emulates the Stripe REST API at the wire level, faithful enough that the real `stripe` Python SDK works unchanged. Difficulty comes from breadth (12+ resource families, list/error envelopes, restricted keys) AND depth on three explicitly named traps with subtle concurrency/temporal semantics (idempotency replay incl. cached errors and same-key serialization, webhook retry/backoff/re-signing, PaymentIntent state machine), all offline against an external contract the agent must reconstruct. This demands heavy, sustained meta-work: deep research of the real Stripe contract, milestone decomposition across a large surface, SDK-driven verification, progress tracking, and course-correction when compatibility breaks.

dimensions.name: Reconstructing the Stripe contract & environment
dimensions.description: Understanding the externally-defined Stripe wire contract (resource shapes, error codes, test PANs, list/idempotency/webhook semantics) and the SDK's expectations before and while building.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The 'spec' is really the real Stripe API; fidelity is graded against SDK behavior the agent must infer, not against this prose. Guessing field names, error codes, or the test-PAN set produces silently non-compliant output.

anchors.0: Starts coding straight from the prompt; invents field names, error codes, and PANs with no reference to actual Stripe behavior.
anchors.3: Recalls a few Stripe shapes from memory; covers the obvious resources but leaves error envelope, list envelope, or PAN set half-guessed.
anchors.5: Establishes the core contract for main resources — object shapes, error `{type,code,...}` mapping, list envelope, the published test-PAN set — and confirms how the SDK sets `api_base`/auth headers before building on them.
anchors.8: Systematically probes the contract for the hard parts too: idempotency key scope `(api_key, key, body)`, webhook signature format, PaymentIntent status transitions, restricted-key scopes — grounded in how the real API/SDK behaves, and revisits sources as gaps surface mid-build.
anchors.10: Sustained, self-correcting reconstruction: cross-checks each subsystem's behavior against concrete SDK round-trips or documented Stripe semantics, catches under-specified corners (decline_code vs code, replay of cached error bodies, re-signing for replay windows) early, and lets findings reshape the design rather than discovering mismatches late.

dimensions.name: Sequencing a large surface + three deep traps
dimensions.description: Breaking the work into an ordered hierarchy — auth/boot skeleton, CRUD resources, then the risk-heavy idempotency/webhook/state-machine subsystems — each with a clear done-condition.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The surface is too large to hold in one push, and the three named traps carry most of the risk; a flat, breadth-first slog will run out of horizon before the hard semantics are correct.

anchors.0: No structure; jumps between endpoints ad hoc with no ordering or done-conditions.
anchors.3: A flat endpoint checklist with no risk prioritization and no explicit 'done' criteria per item.
anchors.5: Clear milestones (boot+auth first, then resource groups, then the traps) with rough done-conditions, and recognizes the three traps as distinct workstreams.
anchors.8: Risk-aware sequencing: gets a bootable auth'd skeleton verifiable early, then deliberately front-loads or ring-fences the high-risk subsystems (idempotency serialization, webhook backoff/re-sign, PI state machine) as first-class milestones each with an explicit check, rather than burying them in CRUD.
anchors.10: Milestone structure that visibly de-risks the whole horizon: dependencies made explicit (e.g. PaymentIntent charges before refunds before subscription invoices), the trickiest semantics scheduled while budget remains, and the plan carries concrete acceptance conditions per milestone that later verification maps onto.

dimensions.name: SDK-driven, offline compatibility checks
dimensions.description: Deliberately designing how correctness is confirmed — exercising routes with the real `stripe` SDK / requests, and building targeted checks for idempotency, webhook retry, and state-machine edge cases — beyond 'it returns 200'.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Wire-level compatibility and the trap semantics fail silently; only active verification (ideally through the SDK the way the verifier will) distinguishes a plausible-looking response from a compliant one.

anchors.0: No verification; assumes endpoints work because the code was written.
anchors.3: Manual curl of a couple of happy paths; no SDK check, no coverage of error bodies or the trap behaviors.
anchors.5: Boots the service, smoke-tests health and several CRUD flows, and checks a few error/edge cases — but leaves the hardest semantics (concurrent idempotent retries, webhook backoff, illegal state transitions) largely unverified.
anchors.8: Verifies through the actual `stripe` SDK against `api_base`, and constructs specific checks for the traps: replaying an idempotency key (incl. a cached error body), same-key-different-body → 400, capturing a succeeded intent → 400, invalid PAN → decline, webhook 5xx retry/backoff.
anchors.10: A deliberate verification harness that covers happy paths, error envelopes, HTTP-code mappings, list pagination, restricted-key 403s, and the concurrency/temporal traps (serialized same-key retries never double-charge, re-signed late webhook deliveries), re-run after changes so regressions are caught rather than assumed away.

dimensions.name: Tracking coverage across a wide surface
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate done-vs-remaining picture over 12+ resource families and the trap subsystems, and detecting when effort is stuck or circling on one behavior.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With this much surface it is easy to lose the plot — over-polishing customers while subscriptions/invoices/webhooks remain unstarted, or re-debugging the same idempotency case repeatedly.

anchors.0: No sense of overall coverage; forgets whole resource families or repeats work.
anchors.3: Vague mental tracking; discovers late that major endpoints or the webhook worker were never implemented.
anchors.5: Keeps a running checklist of endpoints/subsystems and their status, and generally knows what remains.
anchors.8: Actively maintains coverage against the full route table, notices when stuck on one behavior and time-boxes it, and reallocates attention so no major area is silently dropped.
anchors.10: Continuous, accurate accounting across the whole horizon: distinguishes implemented-and-verified from implemented-only from missing, catches thrashing/circular debugging early and names it, and adjusts pace to land the full surface plus the traps within budget.

dimensions.name: Course-correcting on compatibility failures
dimensions.description: Revising design/approach when SDK round-trips, error shapes, or trap semantics diverge from expectations — rather than pressing on with a falsified assumption.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Reconstructing an external contract guarantees wrong initial assumptions (field names, signature scheme, state rules); the agent must let contradicting evidence rewrite the design, sometimes structurally (e.g. how idempotency serialization or the billing worker is built).

anchors.0: Ignores failing SDK calls or wrong outputs; keeps building on the broken assumption.
anchors.3: Patches surface symptoms (tweaks a field) without revisiting the underlying wrong model, so the same class of mismatch recurs.
anchors.5: When a check fails, diagnoses and fixes the root cause for that case and moves on.
anchors.8: Treats divergences as signals about the contract: on discovering e.g. a wrong signature format or state-transition rule, updates the mental model and propagates the fix across related endpoints, not just the one that failed.
anchors.10: Fluid, evidence-driven correction across the horizon, including structural pivots when needed (rethinking idempotency locking, webhook re-signing, or state-machine modeling once reality contradicts the plan), while preserving already-verified work — never barrels ahead on a falsified assumption.
